subject: chemistry-hl
about: Original practice questions written for NevaIB from the IB guide's syllabus understandings and the school's unit order. Not IB past-paper questions, not publisher material and not IB markschemes: the marking points are written for self-marking. Organisms, experiments and data in data-response items are invented for practice.

items.stem: Which is an assumption of the ideal gas model?
choices: The particles occupy most of the volume of the container
Collisions between particles lose kinetic energy
There are no attractive forces between the particles
The particles move only when the gas is heated
items.note: Ideal gas: negligible particle volume, no intermolecular forces, elastic collisions, random motion. Each wrong option contradicts one of these.

items.stem: At constant temperature, the pressure of a fixed amount of gas is doubled. The volume becomes:
items.note: Boyle's law: pV = constant at fixed T and n, so doubling p halves V.

items.stem: Which temperature must be used in gas law calculations?
choices: Celsius, because gas laws were measured in °C
Kelvin, found by adding 273 to the Celsius value
Kelvin, found by subtracting 273 from the Celsius value
Either scale, as long as the same one is used throughout
items.note: Gas laws need absolute temperature: T(K) = T(°C) + 273. Ratios using °C give wrong answers (e.g. doubling 10 °C is not doubling the kinetic energy).

items.stem: What volume does 0.500 mol of an ideal gas occupy at 300 K and 150 kPa? (R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)
items.note: V = nRT/p = 0.500 × 8.31 × 300 ÷ 150 000 Pa = 0.00831 m³ = 8.31 dm³. Use Pa and get m³, then × 1000 for dm³.

items.stem: How many moles of gas are in 2.27 dm³ at STP? (molar volume = 22.7 dm³ mol⁻¹)
items.note: n = V ÷ Vm = 2.27 ÷ 22.7 = 0.100 mol. The data booklet STP is 273 K and 100 kPa.

items.stem: A gas occupies 2.00 dm³ at 300 K and 100 kPa. What is its volume at 400 K and 200 kPa?
A sealed gas syringe is warmed from 20 °C to 40 °C at constant pressure. The volume of gas:
items.note: V ∝ T in kelvin: 313 ÷ 293 = 1.068, about 7%. Doubling the Celsius value does not double the absolute temperature.

items.stem: Real gases deviate most from ideal behaviour at:
items.note: At high pressure the particle volume is no longer negligible; at low temperature intermolecular forces become significant (particles move slowly).

items.stem: 0.640 g of a gas occupies 0.250 dm³ at 298 K and 100 kPa. What is its molar mass? (R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)
items.note: n = pV/RT = (100 000 × 0.000250) ÷ (8.31 × 298) = 0.01010 mol; M = 0.640 ÷ 0.01010 = 63.4 g mol⁻¹. Unit slips give the factor-of-10 distractors.

items.stem: Why does ammonia deviate more from ideal gas behaviour than helium at the same conditions?
choices: Ammonia molecules form hydrogen bonds with each other
Helium atoms are larger than ammonia molecules
Ammonia molecules move faster than helium atoms at the same temperature
Helium atoms attract each other more strongly
items.note: Stronger intermolecular forces (hydrogen bonding in NH₃) make the real gas behave less ideally. He has only very weak London forces.

items.stem: A graph of pV against p for 1 mol of an ideal gas at constant temperature is:
choices: A straight line through the origin
A curve that falls towards zero
A straight line with a negative gradient
items.note: For an ideal gas pV = nRT is constant at fixed n and T, whatever p is, so the graph is horizontal. Real gases curve away from it at high p.

items.stem: State two assumptions of the kinetic theory for an ideal gas.
markscheme: Particles have negligible volume compared with the container (1)
Particles move randomly in straight lines between collisions (1)
items.tactic: State = no explanation needed, but each assumption must be precise ("negligible", not "no" volume).

items.stem: Calculate the volume, in cm³, of hydrogen produced at STP when 0.243 g of magnesium reacts completely with excess hydrochloric acid. Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g). (Ar Mg = 24.31; molar volume = 22.7 dm³ mol⁻¹ at STP)
items.tactic: Mole maps: mass → moles → ratio → volume, one line each.

items.stem: Explain, in terms of particles, why the pressure of a gas in a sealed rigid container increases when it is heated.
markscheme: Particles gain kinetic energy and move faster (1)
They collide with the container walls more frequently (1)
Collisions are with greater force/momentum, so force per unit area (pressure) increases (1)
items.tactic: Pressure explanations need both frequency and force of collisions.

items.stem:
(Invented data for practice.) A student measured the volume of 0.00200 mol of a gas at constant pressure (101 kPa) at different temperatures: 0 °C 44.9 cm³; 25 °C 49.0 cm³; 50 °C 53.2 cm³; 75 °C 57.3 cm³.
(a) Show that the data are consistent with V ∝ T (in K). (b) Use the 25 °C result to calculate a value for R. (c) The expected value of R is 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Calculate the percentage error and suggest one cause.
markscheme: (a) V/T is roughly constant: e.g. 44.9/273 = 0.164 and 57.3/348 = 0.165 cm³ K⁻¹ (1)
Cause: e.g. gas syringe friction / temperature of gas not equal to water bath / reading the scale (1)
items.tactic: Unfamiliar context: find the syllabus idea being tested, quote the data (with units) when you describe a trend, then explain it with that idea. One marking point per linked step.
